name: Vegetotherapy

card.summary: A body-oriented psychotherapy from Wilhelm Reich that uses breathing and work on muscle tension to loosen chronic 'armor', which practitioners link to posture, expression and a more relaxed, open bearing.
card.note: Practised under the Reichian tradition; later orgone theories are separate and contested.

quick.overview:
Vegetotherapy is a form of Reichian psychotherapy developed in the 1930s. It treats chronic muscular tension, which Reich called body armor, as a physical expression of emotional defenses, and works on it through breathing and body work.

Practitioners describe the payoff as looser posture, freer breathing and a more expressive face and body. Research is small: one 2025 randomized trial in soldiers reported lower anxiety and better balance after six weeks of sessions.
quick.how: Sessions traditionally involve lying down in minimal clothing, breathing deeply and rhythmically while the therapist observes or presses on tense areas such as the jaw, neck, chest and abdomen. Later body-psychotherapy schools adapted the approach in varied forms.
quick.risks: Strong emotional release can occur during sessions, and the method's use of touch led to disputes in psychoanalysis. It is a psychotherapy practised by trained therapists; people with trauma histories or psychiatric conditions are generally advised to seek qualified clinical guidance.

lead: Vegetotherapy is a body-oriented psychotherapy created by the psychoanalyst Wilhelm Reich in the 1930s. It grew out of his 'character analysis' and aims to loosen the muscular 'armor' that he believed holds emotional defenses in the body [1][2].

In appearance terms, proponents tie armor to shallow breathing, stiff posture, a rigid face and restricted movement, so releasing it is said to produce easier breathing, a more upright and fluid bearing and a more expressive face [2]. It sits in the same culture as posture and tension-release practices discussed in looksmaxxing communities.
Published research is small. A 2025 randomized controlled trial in 29 soldiers examined a six-week vegetotherapy program for anxiety and balance [3].

chain: Breathing and body work on chronic muscle tension
Less held tension in the neck, jaw, chest and torso
Easier posture and a more relaxed, expressive presence
angle.text: Practitioners describe armor as visible in posture, breathing and facial rigidity, and say releasing it changes how a person holds and carries themselves. This is the tradition's own framing rather than a measured cosmetic outcome.

paras: Vegetotherapy extends Reich's character analysis, which aimed to loosen the character defenses and 'body armor' that sustain neurosis [2]. The name comes from 'vegetative currents', the autonomic sensations Reich believed flowed once armor dissolved [1][2].

Descriptions of the classical method have the patient lie on a bed in underwear and breathe deeply and rhythmically, while the analyst palpates or tickles areas of muscle tension [2]. Reports from the tradition include crying, shouting, trembling and recollection of past experiences thought to be stored emotions [1][2]. Signs of tension in this framework include shallow breathing and poor posture, and natural breathing is taken as a sign of recovery [2].

Reich joined the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society in 1920 and published Character Analysis in 1933 [1][2]. He moved to Oslo in 1934, where vegetotherapy took shape, and emigrated to the United States in 1939 [1]. After he announced the concept of orgone energy, vegetotherapy was succeeded in his work by psychiatric orgone therapy [2]. Reich was expelled from the International Psychoanalytical Association in 1934 [1].
Its body work shaped later approaches such as bioenergetics and biodynamic psychotherapy, as well as neo-Reichian massage [1][2].

The psychoanalyst Otto Fenichel, in 1946, acknowledged positive effects but raised concerns that psychological splitting could keep bodily changes from affecting the mind and that released material still needed working-through [2]. Mainstream psychoanalysis objected to therapeutic touch [1].

A 2025 randomized controlled trial in 29 soldiers (average age 30) compared twice-weekly vegetotherapy for six weeks with no intervention. The treated group reported a 68% reduction in anxiety scores versus 9% in controls, and open-eyes postural balance improved within the treated group, though between-group balance differences were not significant [3]. A survey of Greek psychiatrists lists vegetotherapy among the forms of training some had received, without evaluating its effects [4].
